profile.summary: TraitGym tests whether a model can pick out causal non-coding single-nucleotide variants in the human genome. It has two datasets: causal variants for 113 Mendelian traits and strong causal candidates for 83 complex traits, each paired with matched control variants. It is for people comparing DNA language models, sequence-to-function models and conservation or integrative scores on regulatory variant interpretation.

summary_quotes.text: In this work, we present TraitGym, a curated dataset of regulatory genetic variants that are either known to be causal or are strong candidates across 113 Mendelian and 83 complex traits, along with carefully constructed control variants.

We frame the causal variant prediction task as a binary classification problem and benchmark various models, including functional-genomics-supervised models, self-supervised models, models that combine machine learning predictions with curated annotation features, and ensembles of these.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is binary classification: is a variant putatively causal for any trait or not. Only non-coding single-nucleotide variants are included, because the authors see interpretation of non-coding variants as a key use for DNA sequence models. A model sees the reference and alternate alleles and the surrounding DNA sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4, Benchmark datasets and Task definition

quotes.text: The task is to classify whether a variant is putatively causal for any trait or not. The input data consist of the reference and alternate allele together with the DNA sequence context.
Further, we focus on single-nucleotide variants, the most common form of genetic variation, which is still challenging to interpret.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Mendelian positives are causal non-coding variants for 113 Mendelian diseases from OMIM, with variants above 0.1% minor allele frequency in gnomAD removed; common gnomAD variants are the controls. Complex-trait positives come from statistical fine-mapping of UK Biobank association studies: variants with posterior inclusion probability above 0.9 in any trait. Each positive is matched to 9 controls on chromosome, consequence and distance to the transcription start site; complex-trait controls are also matched on minor allele frequency and LD score. Table 1 gives 338 causal variants among 3,380 for Mendelian traits and 1,140 among 11,400 for complex traits. Larger versions with millions of controls per positive are also provided.

quotes.text: Curated causal non-coding variants for 113 Mendelian diseases were collected from Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man, OMIM
For additional stringency, we filtered out a small percentage of variants with minor allele frequency (MAF) greater than 0.1% in the Genome Aggregation Database, gnomAD
Putative causal and control non-coding variants for 83 complex traits were obtained by processing statistical fine-mapping results
Specifically, we used variants with posterior inclusion probability (PIP) in the credible set greater than 0.9 in any trait as positives and variants with PIP

For each putative causal non-coding variant, we sampled 9 non-coding variants from the control set, matching chromosome, consequence, and distance to transcription start site (TSS). For complex traits, we additionally matched MAF and linkage disequilibrium (LD) score
colspan="1">Mendelian traits3383,380113
colspan="1">Complex traits1,14011,40083
However, we also provide a larger version of the dataset with millions of negative controls per positive variant, for which we evaluate a subset of the models.
We used gnomAD common variants (MAF > 5%) as controls.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are scored zero-shot, or by ridge logistic regression on extracted features (linear probing). Linear probing uses one fold per chromosome: each chromosome is tested with a model trained on the others, and the regularisation is tuned by cross-validation on the training chromosomes. The metric is AUPRC per chromosome, averaged across chromosomes with weights by sample size, with a bootstrap standard error. With 9 controls per positive, a random score has AUPRC 0.1. The README names AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average as the main metric.

quotes.text: As evaluation metric, we calculate the area under the precision recall curve (AUPRC) for each chromosome (for a model trained on the remaining chromosomes), and then compute a weighted average across chromosomes based on sample size, together with a standard error estimated via bootstrapping
The baseline AUPRC is 0.1, which is the proportion of positives.
We evaluate zero-shot model scores as well as ridge logistic regression classifiers (linear probing) trained using extracted features

We use a number of folds equal to the number of chromosomes. In each fold, we test on a single chromosome using a model trained on the remaining chromosomes, and the regularization hyperparameter is chosen based on cross-validation on the training chromosomes
`AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average` (main metric)

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The README says to clone the repository, create the conda environment from workflow/envs/general.yaml, optionally download the precomputed datasets and predictions (6.7G) from Hugging Face into results/dataset, and ask Snakemake for a result path. Your own features go in a parquet file under results/dataset/{dataset}/features/, and Snakemake then computes zero-shot or logistic regression metrics for them. A Colab notebook, TraitGym.ipynb, is also offered.

quotes.text: First, clone the repo and `cd` into it.
conda env create -f workflow/envs/general.yaml
Optionally, download precomputed datasets and predictions (6.7G):
To evaluate your own set of model features, place a dataframe of shape `n_variants,n_features` in `results/dataset/{dataset}/features/{features}.parquet`.
Example notebook to run variant effect prediction with a gLM, runs in 5 min on Google Colab: `TraitGym.ipynb`

strengths.text: Controls are matched to each positive on chromosome, consequence and TSS distance, and for complex traits also on MAF and LD score, so simple confounders are less likely to drive scores.

limitations.text: The authors say it has limited ability to resolve subtle differences in performance; some differences only show on the expanded datasets.

quotes.text: TraitGym was designed to have simple metrics and be tractable to run for even billion parameter models, but has limited ability to resolve subtle differences in performance.

limitations.text: Datasets are small for supervised probes: the authors note overfitting, and several linear probes score worse than zero-shot on Mendelian traits.

quotes.text: It can be challenging to avoid overfitting when training high-dimensional models on this relatively small dataset, and several linear probing models perform worse than zero-shot.
